name: Transformer-GNN Hybrid
analogy: Think of it as a research desk with two questions per market. First: which of this market's own past bars matter right now? Second: which other markets are telling me something? One mechanism answers the first by looking back at the market's own history, and another answers the second by listening to linked markets.

steps.title: Give every instrument a window of history
steps.description: Each instrument gets a window of its recent bars with the same features, computed from past data only. A marker for each bar's position in time is added so the model knows the order.
steps.inExample: MNQ, MES and MYM each get 64 five-minute bars with 8 features.

steps.title: Let each market look back at its own past
steps.description: Attention lets each bar weigh every earlier bar and decide how much each one matters. A strict rule hides future bars, so a bar can only look backward. The same attention settings are used for every instrument.
steps.inExample: In MNQ, the latest bar pays most attention to the high-volume bar 9 bars earlier.

steps.title: Define the links between markets
steps.description: A graph says which instruments are related, using structure such as index family or a shared currency, or a measured recent correlation. Link strength can also be fed to attention as a gentle nudge.
steps.inExample: All three index futures are linked, with the MNQ to MES link strongest at 93 percent correlation.

steps.title: Pass messages between linked markets
steps.description: Each instrument gathers summaries from its linked neighbours and blends them with its own. After this step, each market's summary reflects what related markets are doing.
steps.inExample: MES's summary now includes the sharp selling that appeared first in MNQ.

steps.title: Stack the two operations into layers
steps.description: The look-back step and the message step are repeated in several layers, each adding its result onto the running summary. Stacking lets the model combine own-history clues and neighbour clues in more complex ways.
steps.inExample: Three layers are stacked, each adding both a time and a neighbour contribution.

steps.title: Read out predictions for all markets
steps.description: The final summary at the latest bar of each instrument goes to an output layer that gives a prediction per instrument. The attention and message weights can be kept for inspection.
steps.inExample: The model outputs 45 percent up for MNQ, 46 percent for MES and 51 percent for MYM.

useFor.task: Forecasting direction across a basket of related markets
useFor.example: Predicting the 6-bar direction of MNQ, MES and MYM together, with each prediction informed by the others.

useFor.task: Studying lead and lag between markets
useFor.example: Reading the link weights to see whether MNQ leads MES by a bar or two during selloffs.
Looking far back at the bars around a scheduled release while spreading the effect across linked instruments.
Producing one score per instrument to rank which index future to favour.

avoidWhen: You trade a single market; with no neighbours the graph half adds nothing, and gradient boosting or a plain sequence model costs far less.
You have limited history; attention models need plenty of data and careful warm-up, and a simpler model on engineered features will usually be steadier.

example.scenario: At the close of the 14:35 five-minute bar, the model reads 64 bars of MNQ, MES and MYM and returns a probability of up for each instrument over the next 6 bars.

input.summary: Three instruments, 64 normalised bars each, and a graph of their links.

fields.name: instruments
fields.meaning: Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100, Micro E-mini S&P 500 and Micro E-mini Dow futures, which share a common factor.

fields.name: bars per instrument
fields.meaning: Over five hours of 5-minute bars given to each instrument.

fields.name: MNQ return over the last 6 bars
fields.value: minus a third of a percent
fields.meaning: Recent price change in the instrument that moved first.

fields.name: MNQ average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: Typical high-to-low travel of an MNQ bar.

fields.name: link strength MNQ to MES
fields.meaning: How tightly the two have moved together lately.

fields.name: link strength MNQ to MYM
fields.meaning: A looser link to the third instrument.

output.summary: A probability of up for each instrument plus the weights the model used.

fields.name: MNQ probability of up
fields.meaning: Chance that MNQ's close 6 bars later is higher.

fields.name: MYM probability of up
fields.meaning: The same event for MYM, the least affected.

fields.name: strongest look-back bar for MNQ
fields.meaning: The earlier bar the latest MNQ bar paid most attention to.

example.reading: MNQ and MES lean mildly down and MYM is near even, so the model sees weakness spreading from MNQ. These are small leans; confirm on walk-forward folds with costs, and check against a version without the graph to see whether neighbour information really helps.
